//: MEMORY-RETENTION EVAL — the golden pack (POC-STATE-ASSESSMENT rec 8).
A 20-turn conversation in which the user states TEN things a real user would
state and expect the system to remember: the decision goal, a hard numeric
constraint, a date constraint, an option name with a stated preference for it,
a headcount, a lease preference, a CORRECTION to the headcount, a legal
constraint, a transition constraint, and a scope lock. Then ten turns of
ordinary back-and-forth that state nothing durable.
WHY THE SHAPE IS WHAT IT IS — every number below is derived, not chosen:
* All ten durable statements sit in turns 1-10, and the verbatim window is
CONTEXT_PACK_RECENT_TURNS_CAP (8) turns. Measuring at turn 19 therefore
puts EVERY durable statement OUTSIDE the window, so the retention reading
can only come from the rolling summary. MEM-FLOOR 4 asserts exactly that
rather than trusting the arithmetic.
* measure_at_turns is [19, 20] because shouldRegenerate() regenerates from
full history when turnCount % SUMMARY_REGEN_INTERVAL === 0. Turn 19 is the
end of a nine-pass INCREMENTAL chain (where a loss compounds); turn 20 is a
REGEN from full history (where the estate's anti-compounding guard gets its
chance to repair one).
* The durable statements are ordinary length (~110-140 chars), NOT padded.
That is the point: ten of them, carried verbatim, land BETWEEN the 1,200
target and the 1,600 hard cap, so budget pressure is produced by the real
constants rather than by a tuned fixture. MEM-FLOOR 5 pins that band and
fails loud if editing the pack drifts out of it.
* Every durable statement is exactly ONE sentence ending in a single full
stop — the contract splitStatements() depends on, asserted at load.
ASSISTANT TURNS are deliberately uniform and content-free. A summariser arm
that minted from assistant prose would put GATE 2 (unwitnessed attribution)
in the middle of the measurement; keeping them inert isolates the CONSTRAINTS
carrier, which is what this eval is about.

cases.note: Site-selection decision. Ten durable statements (turns 1-10) then ten ordinary turns.

turns.user: We need to decide where to put our northern distribution hub, and I want a recommendation I can take to the board.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: The total fit-out budget must not go above £180,000 — that is a hard ceiling from finance, not a target, so anything over it is out.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Site works cannot start any earlier than March, because the lease on the current unit in Openshaw runs right up to the end of winter.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Of the three sites I do prefer Bramhall Park, mainly because it is the only one on the shortlist with its own rail siding for inbound pallets.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Plan for at least 25 people on site from day one; that is the number the operations team gave me this morning.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: I would prefer a shorter lease even if the rent per square foot works out higher — we cannot be locked in for ten years on a guess.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Correction on the headcount: it is 40 people, not 25 — I was reading last year's plan when I told you that.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: One more constraint from legal: we must not sign anything before the environmental survey on the site is back and clean.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Whatever we pick has to keep the Leeds depot running for at least six more months, because we cannot cut over both sites at once.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: The shortlist must stay fixed at the three sites we already have, and I do not want new options introduced at this stage.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Can you walk me through how you are weighing these against each other?
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: That makes sense so far, keep going.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: What would move your ranking the most?
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Interesting. And how confident are you in that ordering?
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Okay, noted.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Anything I should be thinking about that I have not raised?
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Fair enough, carry on.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: Right, let us get to a view.
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: So which one do you land on, and why?
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

turns.user: And what should I check before I take this upstairs?
turns.assistant: Understood, I have that on record.

facts.note: The decision itself. Losing this is the first thing a tester notices: the coach no longer knows what is being decided.
A hard number the user called non-negotiable. MEASURED, not floored — see the floor rationale in evaluateFloors.
A date constraint stated once and never repeated.
A named option the user expressed a preference for.
SUPERSEDED by headcount_corrected. Its survival is only a problem if the correction is lost — MEM-FLOOR 2.
A stated preference with an explicit trade-off attached.
The user CORRECTING themselves. Losing a correction is the worst class: the system keeps acting on the withdrawn number.
A blocking precondition from a third party.
An operational constraint naming another site.
A scope instruction. Losing it makes the coach reopen a closed question.
NEGATIVE CONTROL. Never said by anyone. A detector that reports this as retained is reading something other than the conversation, and every other row is void.
